entries.title: The Claims of Christ: His Self-Witness and Implicit Deity
entries.content_summary: Basic Christianity begins with the person of Christ, and Stott argues that the central issue is Jesus' own self-witness. Though Jesus seldom stated his deity in bald propositions, his words and bearing are saturated with implicit and explicit claims that only God could rightly make. He set himself at the center of his message, forgave sins as one wronged by every sin (Mrk.2.5), and made himself the sole way to the Father: 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me' (Jhn.14.6). Most startling are his claims to eternal, divine existence — 'before Abraham was, I am' (Jhn.8.58) — and to unity with the Father: 'I and the Father are one' (Jhn.10.30). Both provoked attempts to stone him for blasphemy. Stott presses the reader to weigh these claims honestly, for they force a verdict.
entries.content_detail:
Stott opens his case for Christianity not with argument about God in the abstract but with the concrete figure of Jesus, and specifically with his self-understanding. The reader, he says, must begin by facing what Jesus claimed. Some of the claims are explicit; many are implicit in the way he spoke and acted, which is in some ways more compelling because less self-conscious.

Jesus placed himself at the center of everything. He called people to himself, promising rest to the weary and making allegiance to him the hinge of human destiny. He assumed the authority to forgive sins — not merely sins committed against himself, but sins as such, as when he told the paralytic, 'Son, your sins are forgiven' (Mrk.2.5), prompting the scribes rightly to ask who but God can forgive sins. He claimed to be humanity's only mediator with God: 'no one comes to the Father except through me' (Jhn.14.6).

Most direct of all are his claims to a divine nature. To hostile questioners he said, 'before Abraham was, I am' (Jhn.8.58), applying to himself the timeless self-designation of God and provoking them to pick up stones. He declared, 'I and the Father are one' (Jhn.10.30), and again they moved to stone him for making himself God. Stott's point is that these claims cannot be filed away as the sayings of a great moral teacher. A merely good teacher does not talk this way about himself. The claims force the classic alternative that Stott, like others, presses: a man who says such things is either deceiving us, or deluded, or telling the truth — a liar, a lunatic, or the Lord he claimed to be. The comfortable option of 'great teacher and nothing more' is precisely the one Jesus' own words rule out, and the rest of the book unfolds from how the reader answers this question.

entries.title: The Character and Resurrection of Christ as Evidence
entries.content_summary: Claims alone prove nothing; Stott asks whether Jesus' claims are corroborated. He points to two lines of evidence: Jesus' character and his resurrection. The character of Jesus is startlingly consistent with his claims — a life of such moral perfection that he could challenge his enemies, 'which one of you convicts me of sin?' (Jhn.8.46), and those closest to him testified he 'committed no sin' (1Pe.2.22). A deluded or dishonest man does not display such humility, integrity, and love. The decisive corroboration is the resurrection. Stott treats it as a historical event on which everything turns: 'if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain' (1Co.15.14). The empty tomb, the transformed disciples, and the birth of the church are, he argues, best explained by the fact that God raised Jesus from the dead.
entries.content_detail:
Having set out Christ's claims, Stott turns to the question of their credibility. Anyone can make grand assertions; the issue is whether the evidence supports them. He offers two principal witnesses: the character of Jesus and his resurrection from the dead.

First, character. Stott argues that the moral portrait of Jesus in the Gospels is impossible to reconcile with the theory that he was either a liar or a deluded fanatic. His teaching set the highest ethical standard the world has known, and he embodied it. He combined qualities rarely found together — strength and gentleness, authority and humility. Above all, he displayed no consciousness of personal sin, no confession, no sense of needing forgiveness, even while calling everyone else to repent. He could openly challenge his opponents, 'which one of you convicts me of sin?' (Jhn.8.46), and those who lived beside him concluded that he 'committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth' (1Pe.2.22). Such sinless self-possession fits the claims of one who is more than a man.

Second, and decisively, the resurrection. Stott presents it as a matter of historical evidence, not mere piety, and stakes the whole of Christianity upon it. Paul himself did so: 'if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain' (1Co.15.14). Stott weighs the data — the sealed and guarded tomb found empty, the failure of anyone to produce the body, the many appearances to witnesses who could be cross-examined, and the sudden transformation of demoralized disciples into fearless heralds willing to die for their testimony. The birth and explosive growth of the church, centered from the first on the claim that God 'raised him up' (Act.2.24), demand an adequate cause. Stott concludes that the resurrection is the best explanation of the facts, and that in raising Jesus God set his seal on his Son's astonishing claims.

entries.title: The Fact and Nature of Sin: Self-Centredness That Separates from God
entries.content_summary: Having established who Christ is, Stott turns to human need, for the gospel is good news only to those who know their plight. He treats sin as a universal fact and a personal condition, not merely a catalog of misdeeds. Every person is implicated: 'all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God' (Rom.3.23). Sin's essence is self-centredness — the dethroning of God and the enthroning of self — and its root is the heart, from which come evil thoughts and deeds (Mrk.7.21). The heart itself is 'deceitful above all things' (Jer.17.9), so we habitually underestimate our condition. The gravest consequence is relational: sin separates us from God. 'Your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God' (Isa.59.2). Stott insists this diagnosis is not pessimism but realism, and that only those who feel the disease will seek the cure.
entries.content_detail:
The second main section of Basic Christianity moves from Christ's person to humanity's need. Stott argues that we cannot appreciate the remedy until we have felt the disease, and so he presses an honest diagnosis of sin. He resists both the modern denial that sin exists and the reduction of sin to isolated bad deeds. Sin is first a universal fact: Scripture's verdict falls on everyone without exception — 'all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God' (Rom.3.23). No one may exempt themselves; the standard is God's own glory, and all fall short of it.

More importantly, Stott probes the nature of sin. Its essence is not merely breaking rules but self-centredness — the reversal of the created order in which God should be at the center and self in orbit around him. In sin, self usurps the throne that belongs to God. This is why Jesus located sin in the heart rather than in circumstances: 'from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts' — and he lists a grim catalog of what the heart produces (Mrk.7.21). The problem is internal, not external; we are not basically good people spoiled by a bad environment but people whose very inclinations are disordered. Jeremiah's diagnosis stands: 'the heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick' (Jer.17.9) — so deceitful that it hides its own condition from us, and we consistently think better of ourselves than the truth warrants.

The most serious consequence of sin, in Stott's account, is neither guilt-feelings nor social harm but separation from God. 'Your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you' (Isa.59.2). Sin ruptures the relationship for which we were made, leaving us estranged and under judgment. This, Stott says, is the predicament the gospel addresses. His purpose is not to depress the reader but to be truthful, for only those who recognize their lost condition will seek and value a Savior.

entries.title: The Work of Christ: Bearing Our Sin in Our Place
entries.content_summary: How does Christ's death meet our need? Stott's answer is substitution: Christ bore our sins in our place. He came not merely as teacher or example but as Savior, and the Savior deals with sin by taking it upon himself. Peter states it plainly: Christ 'himself bore our sins in his body on the tree' (1Pe.2.24) and 'suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God' (1Pe.3.18). Paul reaches the same center: 'for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God' (2Co.5.21). The sinless one was identified with our sin so that we might be identified with his righteousness. This great exchange, foreshadowed in Isaiah's Suffering Servant on whom the LORD laid our iniquity (Isa.53.6), is for Stott the heart of what the cross accomplished.
entries.content_detail:
At the heart of Basic Christianity stands the cross, and Stott interprets it in terms of substitution: Christ died in our place, bearing the sin and its consequences that were ours. He is emphatic that Jesus did not come merely to teach or to inspire but to save, and that salvation required him to deal with the sin that separates us from God. The only way to remove that barrier was for Christ to bear it himself.

Stott gathers the New Testament's witness. Peter writes that Christ 'himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness' (1Pe.2.24) — a deliberate echo of Isaiah 53, presenting Christ as the sin-bearer. Again Peter says he 'suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God' (1Pe.3.18): the innocent in the place of the guilty, with reconciliation as the goal. Most striking is Paul's formulation of the exchange: 'for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God' (2Co.5.21). Stott handles this carefully. Christ was personally sinless — he 'knew no sin' — yet God treated him as sin for us, identifying him with our guilt so completely that its penalty fell on him; and in return the righteousness of God becomes ours in him.

Stott traces this pattern back to Isaiah's Suffering Servant, on whom 'the LORD has laid the iniquity of us all' (Isa.53.6), showing that the New Testament reads the cross through that prophecy. The result is a divine exchange at the center of the gospel: our sin transferred to Christ, his righteousness credited to us. This, Stott insists, is not an arbitrary arrangement but the costly means by which a holy God can justly forgive. What we could never do — remove our own guilt — Christ did on the cross, in our place. Only against this dark background of sin borne does the summons to respond make sense.

entries.title: Counting the Cost: Repentance and Faith
entries.content_summary: For Stott, the gospel demands a response, and that response is costly. He warns against a cheap Christianity that wants the benefits of Christ without submission to his lordship. To become a Christian is to repent and believe — to turn decisively from sin and self-rule and to trust and follow Christ as Lord. Jesus never concealed the cost: 'if anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me' (Mrk.8.34). Discipleship means the abdication of self and the enthronement of Christ. Faith is not mere intellectual assent but wholehearted commitment, confessed openly: 'if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved' (Rom.10.9). Stott urges the seeker to count the cost honestly, for Christ asks for nothing less than everything.
entries.content_detail:
In the final section, Basic Christianity turns from information to decision. Stott insists that Christianity is not a set of ideas to be admired but a Person to be received, and that receiving him carries a real cost that must be weighed in advance. He is sharply critical of any presentation that offers forgiveness and heaven while quietly omitting repentance and the lordship of Christ. To respond to the gospel is to repent and to believe — the two are inseparable.

Repentance, Stott explains, is more than regret; it is a deliberate turning away from everything known to be wrong — from sins, from self-centredness, and from the right to run one's own life. It touches the will, not merely the emotions. Faith is its positive counterpart: a personal trust in Christ that commits the whole person to him. Stott is careful to distinguish saving faith from bare intellectual assent; even the demons believe that God exists. Real faith surrenders and follows.

Jesus himself set the terms without softening them: 'if anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me' (Mrk.8.34). Stott reads self-denial as the dethroning of self and cross-bearing as a daily readiness to die to one's own will in order to obey Christ. Following is the ongoing obedience that flows from that surrender. Because Christ is Lord, the response he requires is nothing partial; he claims the whole of life. Faith must also be public: Paul makes open confession part of the response — 'if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved' (Rom.10.9). Stott therefore urges the reader to face the cost soberly, not to be deterred by it but to embrace it clear-eyed, since what Christ offers infinitely outweighs what he asks us to surrender.

entries.title: Reaching a Decision: Opening the Door and Receiving Christ
entries.content_summary: Stott closes with the summons to a definite decision. Christianity, he argues, cannot remain a matter of drifting interest; at some point the seeker must actively receive Christ. He fastens on the image of Christ standing at the door: 'behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in' (Rev.3.20). Christ will not force an entrance; the handle is on the inside. Salvation becomes personal when the individual opens the door and welcomes him. John states the same truth as receiving: 'to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God' (Jhn.1.12). Stott stresses that this step, though it may be quiet, is decisive, can be made in a prayer of surrender, and issues in a new relationship and the assurance of belonging to Christ.
entries.content_detail:
Stott ends Basic Christianity by pressing for an actual decision, since a book about Christ that produced only admiration would have failed. Faith, he argues, must become personal and definite; the seeker must move from considering Christ to receiving him. He grants that the manner may vary — for some a memorable crisis, for others a quiet and gradual step — but a real transaction of the will is required either way.

His governing image is drawn from the risen Christ's words to the church at Laodicea: 'behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me' (Rev.3.20). Stott draws out its logic with care. Christ has come and taken the initiative; he stands, he knocks, he speaks. But he does not break the door down. The decision to open lies with the individual, and the handle, so to speak, is on the inside. To become a Christian is consciously to open the door and welcome Christ as Savior and Lord into the center of one's life.

The Gospel of John describes the same act as receiving: 'to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God' (Jhn.1.12). Believing and receiving are two sides of one response, and the outcome is a new status — adoption into God's family. Stott suggests that the seeker may make this response through a simple prayer of penitence and surrender, inviting Christ in. He is realistic about the cost already counted, and equally clear about the result: a personal relationship with the living Christ and the beginnings of assurance, grounded not on shifting feelings but on Christ's own promise to come in to all who open the door. The book thus ends not with an argument but with an appeal to decide, echoing the summons to confess Jesus as Lord (Rom.10.9).
